question: What is the health check path for the Palisade admin API?
prompt:
EVIDENCE
[1] [id=slack-eng-palisade-035 | slack message in #eng-palisade | by Nils Berg | on 2027-06-20]
The Palisade admin API is checked by the same process monitor as the gateway, so it has no health check path of its own.

[2] [id=slack-eng-palisade-031 | slack message in #eng-palisade | by Anna Kowalski | on 2027-05-29]
Is the health check path for the Palisade gateway still /health, or did that move when we split the ports?

[3] [id=slack-eng-palisade-024 | slack message in #eng-palisade | by Priya Raman | on 2027-02-11]
For the runbook: the Palisade gateway health check path is /healthz/gateway. It has been that since the first deploy and it is not changing.

[4] [id=slack-eng-palisade-032 | slack message in #eng-palisade | by Nils Berg | on 2027-06-11]
Idea for the next major: move the Palisade gateway health check path to /healthz/v2 and keep the old one as a redirect. Nobody has agreed to this.

[5] [id=slack-eng-core-004 | slack message in #eng-core | by Nils Berg | on 2027-05-20]
Answering the same question for the third time: the Palisade gateway admin API is served on the admin port and requires an mTLS client certificate. No token, no basic auth, a certificate.

[6] [id=doc-057 | document | by Sofia Marchetti | on 2027-06-21 | titled Palisade product notes for the second half of the year]
3 is the release the admin API work lands in. It has no general availability date and will not get one before the summer freeze is over, because putting a date on it now would only be a date we later move. The edge tier gets no feature work this half. It is stable, it is well understood, and every hour spent on it is an hour not spent on the admin API. The exception is anything an incident forces on us. We are not adding a region this year.

[7] [id=slack-eng-relay-026 | slack message in #eng-relay | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-02-12]
The Relay pipeline health check path is /healthz/relay. Different service, different path, please do not copy one into the other.

[8] [id=slack-eng-palisade-025 | slack message in #eng-palisade | by Anna Kowalski | on 2027-05-19]
WRN-4501 is against the admin api component, not the edge nodes. The allow list for admin api client certificates is what failed.

[9] [id=slack-eng-core-026 | slack message in #eng-core | by Priya Raman | on 2027-06-18]
Someone asked whether the Palisade gateway admin API takes a bearer token. Adding token auth beside the certificate has been suggested and not agreed.

[10] [id=doc-057 | document | by Sofia Marchetti | on 2027-06-21 | titled Palisade product notes for the second half of the year]
This is the shape of the Palisade plan for the rest of the year, written after the June planning session. It is a plan and it will move, which is why it is a note and not a commitment. The theme for the second half is the admin API. It is the oldest part of the product, it is the part customers integrate with most deeply, and it is the part with the least written down about it. The work is a rewrite of the authentication path first and the rest afterwards.

[11] [id=issue-wrn-4501 | issue issue-wrn-4501 in project palisade | by Anna Kowalski | on 2027-05-18 | titled WRN-4501 Admin API access denied after a certificate renewal]
Northwind Bank could not reach the Palisade admin API after their client certificate was renewed. Their new certificate was not in our allow list. This is on us: the allow list is manual and nobody updated it.

[12] [id=doc-060 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-16 | titled Palisade gateway ports, the sandbox row]
The sandbox listen port for the Palisade gateway is 8445 and its sandbox admin port is 9445. Production and staging have their own rows on the main ports page.

[13] [id=doc-006 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-16 | titled Palisade gateway ports by environment]
One row per environment, kept here because people keep asking in the channel.

environment | listen port | admin port
----------- | ----------- | ----------
production  | 8443        | 9443
staging     | 8444        | 9444
sandbox     | 8445        | 9445

The listen port is what a customer connects to. The admin port is internal only and is firewalled off.

[14] [id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
To add a node, run the provisioning job with the region flag and wait for the health check to pass twice in a row. Draining a node takes the node out of the load balancer, waits for in-flight requests and then stops the process. The drain timeout is 120 seconds. A node that has not drained by then is killed, and the requests it was serving are lost, so drain during a quiet window if you can choose.

[15] [id=slack-eng-core-015 | slack message in #eng-core | by Tomas Ruiz | on 2027-01-07]
The platform team owns the edge nodes and the admin api. Those are the two components on our page.

[16] [id=doc-config-error-budget | document | by Priya Raman | on 2027-06-05 | titled error budget for the Palisade gateway, applied configuration]
Pasting what is actually deployed, from 5 June 2027. The error budget for the Palisade gateway is the field below.

{
  "setting": "error budget for the Palisade gateway",
  "value": 0.25,
  "effective_from": "2027-06-05",
  "changed_by": "Priya Raman"
}

If the dashboard disagrees with this block, the dashboard is stale.

What is the health check path for the Palisade admin API?

string

question: For how many days does the Palisade audit log keep an entry with no customer attached, in days?
prompt:
EVIDENCE
[1] [id=slack-eng-core-034 | slack message in #eng-core | by Priya Raman | on 2027-02-18]
The Palisade audit log records an actor and an action for every entry. Those are the two fields it has.

[2] [id=slack-eng-core-008 | slack message in #eng-core | by Priya Raman | on 2027-02-17]
The Palisade audit log follows the customer's own data retention window. It is not a separate setting and there is no separate number to look up.

[3] [id=slack-eng-core-036 | slack message in #eng-core | by Nils Berg | on 2027-06-19]
The Palisade audit log does not record a request body and never will, for the obvious reason. Its fields are unchanged.

[4] [id=slack-eng-core-035 | slack message in #eng-core | by Priya Raman | on 2027-04-26]
The Palisade audit log records a resource as well from today, so its fields are actor, action and resource.

[5] [id=slack-data-platform-011 | slack message in #data-platform | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-02-18]
The data retention window that the audit log follows is the one recorded on the customer's contract, not the one in the pipeline config.

[6] [id=slack-eng-core-005 | slack message in #eng-core | by Nils Berg | on 2027-02-10]
Thread on the Palisade audit log store: the options are the existing Postgres cluster, a dedicated Postgres cluster or ClickHouse. Write volume is the deciding factor and nobody has measured it yet.

[7] [id=slack-eng-core-006 | slack message in #eng-core | by Priya Raman | on 2027-02-13]
Closing the audit log thread: we go with a dedicated Postgres cluster for the Palisade audit log. My call, I will own it. ClickHouse is the right answer at ten times this volume and we are not there.

[8] [id=slack-eng-palisade-036 | slack message in #eng-palisade | by Nils Berg | on 2027-03-02]
The Palisade gateway request id header is x-wrenfield-request-id and every log line carries it.

[9] [id=doc-011 | document | by Yusuf Demir | on 2027-03-12 | titled Northwind Bank, audit window]
Northwind Bank hold an annual audit window from 2027-09-01 to 2027-09-30. During that window every access to their tenant is logged with a reason and the logs go to them.

[10] [id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
Certificates are distributed by the platform team and are the same across all edge nodes in a region. A certificate problem is never a single-node problem: if one node is serving a bad certificate, all of them are, and the fix is a redistribution rather than a restart. The log retention on an edge node is 7 days locally, and everything is shipped to the central store where the retention is the customer's own retention window.

[11] [id=slack-security-003 | slack message in #security | by Anna Kowalski | on 2027-06-21]

Standing issue for the Palisade edge cache TTL. Every change to it is recorded as a comment here so support and the docs team have one place to look. Do not close this while the review is running.

[14] [id=slack-general-064 | slack message in #general | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-04-23]

[7] [id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
The Palisade gateway runs on edge nodes in three regions. This runbook covers the edge nodes only: the control plane has its own runbook and the two are deliberately kept apart so an edge problem cannot be fixed by someone who has only read about the control plane. Each region runs at least 4 edge nodes behind a network load balancer. Scaling is manual: there is no autoscaler on the edge tier, on purpose, because a scale event during an incident has bitten us twice.

[8] [id=slack-infra-018 | slack message in #infra | by Ravi Iyer | on 2027-03-19]
eu-west is a customer facing region, so the edge node floor in the runbook applies to it in full. FRA1 carries no customer traffic and is exempt.

[9] [id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
To add a node, run the provisioning job with the region flag and wait for the health check to pass twice in a row. Draining a node takes the node out of the load balancer, waits for in-flight requests and then stops the process. The drain timeout is 120 seconds. A node that has not drained by then is killed, and the requests it was serving are lost, so drain during a quiet window if you can choose.

[10] [id=slack-infra-031 | slack message in #infra | by Ravi Iyer | on 2027-03-24]
ap-south runs 3 Palisade edge nodes, which is below the floor and is a known exception signed off by Ingrid Halvorsen.

[11] [id=doc-054 | document | by Nils Berg | on 2027-01-12 | titled Glossary of Wrenfield terms]
The words we use, written down because a new joiner asked and nobody could point at anything. Edge node: one of the machines that terminates a customer connection to the Palisade gateway. Edge nodes are stateless and are replaced rather than repaired. Control plane: the part of Palisade that configures the edge nodes. It is not on the request path and an incident on it is usually invisible to customers.

[12] [id=slack-infra-030 | slack message in #infra | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-03-20]
The runbook floor is 4 edge nodes for a customer facing region and we hold to it, exceptions in writing only.

Certificates are distributed by the platform team and are the same across all edge nodes in a region. A certificate problem is never a single-node problem: if one node is serving a bad certificate, all of them are, and the fix is a redistribution rather than a restart. The log retention on an edge node is 7 days locally, and everything is shipped to the central store where the retention is the customer's own retention window.

The rotation is done one region at a time, eu-west first, then us-east, then ap-south, with 15 minutes between regions to watch the error rate. [14] [id=doc-046 | document | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-03-15 | titled Relay operations guide, running a backfill]
The backfill runs at a reduced rate so the live pipeline is not starved. The reduced rate is 200 records a second, which is a quarter of what the pipeline does at full speed. [1] [id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
The Palisade gateway runs on edge nodes in three regions. This runbook covers the edge nodes only: the control plane has its own runbook and the two are deliberately kept apart so an edge problem cannot be fixed by someone who has only read about the control plane. Each region runs at least 4 edge nodes behind a network load balancer. Scaling is manual: there is no autoscaler on the edge tier, on purpose, because a scale event during an incident has bitten us twice.

[4] [id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
Certificates are distributed by the platform team and are the same across all edge nodes in a region. A certificate problem is never a single-node problem: if one node is serving a bad certificate, all of them are, and the fix is a redistribution rather than a restart. The log retention on an edge node is 7 days locally, and everything is shipped to the central store where the retention is the customer's own retention window.

[4] [id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
Postmortems are blameless and are readable by the whole company. An incident that produced no customer-visible symptom needs no postmortem, only a line in the weekly digest. The escalation ladder for an incident that is not moving is: incident commander, then the engineering manager on the affected team, then the VP of engineering. Do not skip a rung, and do not escalate by direct message.

[5] [id=doc-041 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Postmortem policy, threshold]
The postmortem threshold is 30 minutes of customer-visible downtime. Under that, a line in the weekly digest is enough. Teams write postmortems under the threshold when they want to, and that does not change the rule.

[6] [id=doc-053 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-06 | titled Wrenfield onboarding guide for new engineers]
Welcome. This guide is what you read in your first week, and it is deliberately short on process and long on where things are. Your manager will have booked the training your team runs; everything else is here. Wrenfield sells two products. Palisade is the API gateway that sits in front of a customer's own services, and it is the older of the two. Relay moves records between a customer system and our store, and it is the one that grew fastest last year.

[7] [id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
The first customer-facing update goes out within 20 minutes of the incident being declared, and every following update goes out at most every 30 minutes until the incident is closed. Support sends those updates; engineering does not write to customers directly during an incident. After the incident, a written postmortem is due within 5 working days. The postmortem names the trigger, the contributing causes and the actions, and every action has an owner and a date.

[8] [id=doc-053 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-06 | titled Wrenfield onboarding guide for new engineers]
The two share nothing but the deployment tooling, and an engineer usually works on one of them. Everything is written down in the channel it belongs to. There is no wiki that is kept up to date and we have stopped pretending otherwise: decisions live in the channel where they were made, with a note in the meeting minutes if a meeting made them. If you cannot find something, ask in the channel rather than by direct message, so the answer is written down for the next person.

[9] [id=doc-008 | document | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-02-02 | titled Wrenfield data processing agreement, summary for engineers]
This is the plain summary of the data processing agreement that every Wrenfield customer contract includes. It is written for engineers, it is not the contract, and where the two disagree the contract wins. Legal keeps the authoritative version. Customer data is processed in the region the customer selects at onboarding. The regions we offer are eu-west, us-east and ap-south.

To add a node, run the provisioning job with the region flag and wait for the health check to pass twice in a row. Draining a node takes the node out of the load balancer, waits for in-flight requests and then stops the process. The drain timeout is 120 seconds. A node that has not drained by then is killed, and the requests it was serving are lost, so drain during a quiet window if you can choose.

question: At how many records a second does a Relay backfill run?
prompt:
EVIDENCE
[1] [id=doc-046 | document | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-03-15 | titled Relay operations guide, running a backfill]
The backfill runs at a reduced rate so the live pipeline is not starved. The reduced rate is 200 records a second, which is a quarter of what the pipeline does at full speed. A backfill at full speed has caused two of the stalls we have had this year. A backfill is never run during the nightly reconciliation window. The reconciliation job and a backfill writing to the same store at the same time produce duplicates that nobody can untangle afterwards, and the replay tool does not deduplicate.

[2] [id=doc-046 | document | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-03-15 | titled Relay operations guide, running a backfill]
A backfill replays historical records through the Relay pipeline for one customer. It is the most dangerous routine thing we do, because it writes to the same store as the live pipeline, and this guide exists so it is done the same way every time. Before anything, the customer is told. A backfill changes what they see in their own reports and they have asked us more than once not to surprise them. The notice goes out from the account owner, at least 3 working days before the backfill starts.

[3] [id=slack-eng-relay-053 | slack message in #eng-relay | by Anna Kowalski | on 2027-06-10]

Written after the change on 8 April 2027. One row per environment.

environment    | Relay dead letter replay batch size
-------------- | ------------
production     | 500 records
staging        | 200 records

Production is the one that counts. Staging is left alone on purpose.

[9] [id=slack-eng-relay-005 | slack message in #eng-relay | by Nils Berg | on 2027-03-15]
Floating an idea for next quarter: take the Relay ingest batch size to 4000 records. Nobody has decided anything, I want to know if it is even possible.

[10] [id=doc-010 | document | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-03-01 | titled Relay pipeline architecture notes]
That buffer is the only place where records live outside a stage. The pipeline is single-tenant: every customer gets their own pipeline instance, and one customer's back pressure cannot slow another customer down. That costs us money and we have decided it is worth it. Failures in fetch are retried with an exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds. Failures in load are not retried inside the pipeline at all: they go to the dead letter queue and are replayed by hand.

[11] [id=issue-wrn-4265 | issue issue-wrn-4265 in project relay | by Anna Kowalski | on 2027-03-01 | titled WRN-4265 Nightly reconciliation misses the last hour of records]
Kestrel Health report that the nightly reconciliation for their Relay pipeline misses the last hour of records roughly once a week. They notice it because their own daily count is short. Their pipeline is single tenant like everyone else's.

[12] [id=slack-eng-relay-066 | slack message in #eng-relay | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-02-06]

[13] [id=slack-eng-relay-060 | slack message in #eng-relay | by Nils Berg | on 2027-05-06]
Floating an idea for next quarter: take the Relay dead letter replay batch size to 1000 records. Nobody has decided anything, I want to know if it is even possible.

[14] [id=doc-010 | document | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-03-01 | titled Relay pipeline architecture notes]
Normalise turns whatever the customer sent into the internal record shape. Validate rejects records that cannot be loaded and writes them to the dead letter queue with the reason attached. Load writes to the store in batches. Back pressure is handled between normalise and validate, and nowhere else. When validate falls behind, normalise blocks, and fetch keeps its own buffer of at most 50000 records before it stops asking the customer system for more.

[15] [id=slack-eng-relay-001 | slack message in #eng-relay | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-01-18]
Decision from the review: Relay ingest batch size is 500 records, effective today, 18 January 2027. Please stop quoting the old figure at customers.

number

question: Within how many hours does the Wrenfield data processing agreement require a customer to be told about a breach?
prompt:
EVIDENCE
[1] [id=doc-008 | document | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-02-02 | titled Wrenfield data processing agreement, summary for engineers]
A deletion request covers the primary store and the search index. Backups are not rewritten: they age out on their own schedule, which is 90 days, and the agreement says so explicitly so nobody promises a customer something we cannot do. Breach notification to the customer is within 72 hours of Wrenfield becoming aware of a breach that affects their data. That clock is not negotiable and it is shorter than the one in the standard terms because two large customers asked for it.

[2] [id=doc-008 | document | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-02-02 | titled Wrenfield data processing agreement, summary for engineers]
This is the plain summary of the data processing agreement that every Wrenfield customer contract includes. It is written for engineers, it is not the contract, and where the two disagree the contract wins. Legal keeps the authoritative version. Customer data is processed in the region the customer selects at onboarding. The regions we offer are eu-west, us-east and ap-south.

[3] [id=slack-data-platform-014 | slack message in #data-platform | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-02-03]
The standard data annex sets breach notification to the customer at 72 hours from us becoming aware. The negotiated annex does not change that number, it changes the sub-processor notice.

[4] [id=slack-data-platform-013 | slack message in #data-platform | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-03-06]
Which data annex a customer is on decides their breach notification clock and their notice periods. There is no per customer override on top of the annex, so Kestrel Health get whatever their annex says.

[5] [id=slack-general-020 | slack message in #general | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-03-07]
To be explicit about the other clauses: the negotiated data annex does not change breach notification, which stays at 72 hours, and it does not change the deletion window.

[6] [id=doc-054 | document | by Nils Berg | on 2027-01-12 | titled Glossary of Wrenfield terms]
It is a number we agreed with ourselves and not something in a contract. Annex: the part of a customer contract that covers data processing. Most customers are on the standard one and a couple negotiated their own.

[7] [id=doc-023 | document | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-03-05 | titled Negotiated data annex, differences from the standard]
The negotiated annex changes one clause. Sub-processor notice is 60 days instead of the standard 30 days. Breach notification to the customer stays at 72 hours, the same as the standard annex, and the deletion window is unchanged. Everything else is the standard text.

[8] [id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
The first customer-facing update goes out within 20 minutes of the incident being declared, and every following update goes out at most every 30 minutes until the incident is closed. Support sends those updates; engineering does not write to customers directly during an incident. After the incident, a written postmortem is due within 5 working days. The postmortem names the trigger, the contributing causes and the actions, and every action has an owner and a date.

question: Within how many days does the Wrenfield data processing agreement answer a deletion request?
prompt:
EVIDENCE
[1] [id=slack-data-platform-023 | slack message in #data-platform | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-05-27]
From memory the deletion request window in the data processing agreement is 30 days, same as the sub-processor notice. Worth checking.

[2] [id=doc-008 | document | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-02-02 | titled Wrenfield data processing agreement, summary for engineers]
A deletion request covers the primary store and the search index. Backups are not rewritten: they age out on their own schedule, which is 90 days, and the agreement says so explicitly so nobody promises a customer something we cannot do. Breach notification to the customer is within 72 hours of Wrenfield becoming aware of a breach that affects their data. That clock is not negotiable and it is shorter than the one in the standard terms because two large customers asked for it.

[3] [id=doc-008 | document | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-02-02 | titled Wrenfield data processing agreement, summary for engineers]
A customer on eu-west has their data stored and processed in eu-west only, and support staff outside the European Union do not get access to it without a written approval from the customer. Sub-processors are listed on the public trust page and customers are told 30 days before a new one is added. A customer may object in writing during those 30 days, and an objection pauses the addition for that customer until it is resolved. Deletion requests are answered within 14 days.

[4] [id=slack-data-platform-020 | slack message in #data-platform | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-02-02]
A deletion request covers the primary store and the search index. Backups are not rewritten: they age out on their own 90 day schedule and the agreement says so explicitly.

[5] [id=slack-data-platform-021 | slack message in #data-platform | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-02-04]
Engineering confirms what the agreement says about a deletion request and the backups: we have no tool that rewrites or edits a backup, and we are not building one.

[6] [id=doc-054 | document | by Nils Berg | on 2027-01-12 | titled Glossary of Wrenfield terms]
It is a number we agreed with ourselves and not something in a contract. Annex: the part of a customer contract that covers data processing. Most customers are on the standard one and a couple negotiated their own.

[7] [id=doc-023 | document | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-03-05 | titled Negotiated data annex, differences from the standard]
The negotiated annex changes one clause. Sub-processor notice is 60 days instead of the standard 30 days. Breach notification to the customer stays at 72 hours, the same as the standard annex, and the deletion window is unchanged. Everything else is the standard text.

[8] [id=doc-056 | document | by Ravi Menon | on 2027-05-04 | titled Customer questions we answer the same way every time]
The limit is per tier and the numbers are in the channel rather than on a public page, so quote the number for their tier and nothing else. Can you delete everything about us? Yes, within the deletion window in the agreement, and it covers the primary store and the search index. Backups age out on their own schedule and we do not rewrite them. Say that plainly rather than hoping it does not come up. When will my bug be fixed? Support does not answer this one.

[9] [id=slack-general-020 | slack message in #general | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-03-07]
To be explicit about the other clauses: the negotiated data annex does not change breach notification, which stays at 72 hours, and it does not change the deletion window.

[10] [id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
The first customer-facing update goes out within 20 minutes of the incident being declared, and every following update goes out at most every 30 minutes until the incident is closed. Support sends those updates; engineering does not write to customers directly during an incident. After the incident, a written postmortem is due within 5 working days. The postmortem names the trigger, the contributing causes and the actions, and every action has an owner and a date.

question: Within how many minutes of an incident being declared does the first customer-facing update have to go out, according to the engineering handbook?
prompt:
EVIDENCE
[1] [id=slack-incidents-031 | slack message in #incidents | by Anna Kowalski | on 2027-06-09]

[2] [id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
The first customer-facing update goes out within 20 minutes of the incident being declared, and every following update goes out at most every 30 minutes until the incident is closed. Support sends those updates; engineering does not write to customers directly during an incident. After the incident, a written postmortem is due within 5 working days. The postmortem names the trigger, the contributing causes and the actions, and every action has an owner and a date.

[3] [id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
The person who confirms it declares the incident in the incidents channel and takes the incident commander role until they hand it over explicitly. The incident commander is not expected to fix anything: the role is to keep the timeline, decide what is communicated and decide when the incident is over. A scribe is appointed for any incident that runs longer than 30 minutes. Communication is on a fixed clock.

[4] [id=slack-incidents-011 | slack message in #incidents | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20]
The handbook names two roles in an incident: the incident commander and, for anything over 30 minutes, the scribe. Support sends the customer updates but that is not an incident role.

The rotation is done one region at a time, eu-west first, then us-east, then ap-south, with 15 minutes between regions to watch the error rate. question: How many records at most does the Relay fetch stage buffer before it stops asking the customer system for more?
prompt:

[1] [id=slack-eng-relay-053 | slack message in #eng-relay | by Anna Kowalski | on 2027-06-10]

[2] [id=doc-010 | document | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-03-01 | titled Relay pipeline architecture notes]
Normalise turns whatever the customer sent into the internal record shape. Validate rejects records that cannot be loaded and writes them to the dead letter queue with the reason attached. Load writes to the store in batches. Back pressure is handled between normalise and validate, and nowhere else. When validate falls behind, normalise blocks, and fetch keeps its own buffer of at most 50000 records before it stops asking the customer system for more.

[3] [id=doc-010 | document | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-03-01 | titled Relay pipeline architecture notes]
That buffer is the only place where records live outside a stage. The pipeline is single-tenant: every customer gets their own pipeline instance, and one customer's back pressure cannot slow another customer down. That costs us money and we have decided it is worth it. Failures in fetch are retried with an exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds. Failures in load are not retried inside the pipeline at all: they go to the dead letter queue and are replayed by hand.

[4] [id=slack-eng-relay-065 | slack message in #eng-relay | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-05-25]
The Relay load stage concurrency is 2 workers and is deliberately lower than the fetch stage, because the store does not like the write burst.

[2] [id=slack-incidents-021 | slack message in #incidents | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20]
A scribe is appointed for any incident that runs longer than 30 minutes. The incident commander does not keep the timeline themselves once a scribe is on.

[3] [id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
The person who confirms it declares the incident in the incidents channel and takes the incident commander role until they hand it over explicitly. The incident commander is not expected to fix anything: the role is to keep the timeline, decide what is communicated and decide when the incident is over. A scribe is appointed for any incident that runs longer than 30 minutes. Communication is on a fixed clock.

[4] [id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
The first customer-facing update goes out within 20 minutes of the incident being declared, and every following update goes out at most every 30 minutes until the incident is closed. Support sends those updates; engineering does not write to customers directly during an incident. After the incident, a written postmortem is due within 5 working days. The postmortem names the trigger, the contributing causes and the actions, and every action has an owner and a date.

[5] [id=slack-incidents-011 | slack message in #incidents | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20]
The handbook names two roles in an incident: the incident commander and, for anything over 30 minutes, the scribe. Support sends the customer updates but that is not an incident role.

Asked in the retro: no, communications lead is not a role in our handbook. It is the incident commander and the scribe.

A written postmortem is required for any incident with more than 30 minutes of customer-visible downtime. It is due within 5 working days of the incident closing. An incident with no customer-visible symptom needs a line in the weekly digest and nothing else.

The rotation is done one region at a time, eu-west first, then us-east, then ap-south, with 15 minutes between regions to watch the error rate. If the error rate moves at all, stop and redistribute the old certificate rather than carrying on. After the rotation, the old certificate stays in the store for 30 days so a rollback is possible, and then it is deleted. Nobody has ever needed the rollback and we keep the 30 days anyway.

question: Who is the second rung of the escalation ladder for an incident on the edge nodes?
prompt:
EVIDENCE
[1] [id=doc-034 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-06 | titled Who the escalation ladder means by the engineering manager]
The second rung of the escalation ladder is the engineering manager of the affected team, and this is who that is. Tomas Ruiz manages the platform team, which owns the edge nodes. Lukas Fenn is the tech lead of the relay team. Ravi Menon manages support.

[2] [id=slack-incidents-009 | slack message in #incidents | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-21]
The escalation ladder is: incident commander, then the engineering manager of the affected team, then me. Do not skip a rung and do not escalate by direct message.

[3] [id=slack-incidents-023 | slack message in #incidents | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-21]
The escalation ladder is incident commander, then the engineering manager of the affected team, then me. Do not skip a rung and do not escalate by direct message.

[4] [id=slack-eng-core-009 | slack message in #eng-core | by Tomas Ruiz | on 2027-05-05]
Ownership, once more, because it comes up in every incident: the edge nodes belong to the platform team.

[5] [id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
Postmortems are blameless and are readable by the whole company. An incident that produced no customer-visible symptom needs no postmortem, only a line in the weekly digest. The escalation ladder for an incident that is not moving is: incident commander, then the engineering manager on the affected team, then the VP of engineering. Do not skip a rung, and do not escalate by direct message.

[6] [id=slack-infra-016 | slack message in #infra | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08]
Worth repeating before it bites us in a gateway incident: distributing a certificate to the edge nodes is not an on-call job. It belongs to whichever team owns the edge nodes, and a bad certificate on the edge is always a distribution problem.

[7] [id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
The Palisade gateway runs on edge nodes in three regions. This runbook covers the edge nodes only: the control plane has its own runbook and the two are deliberately kept apart so an edge problem cannot be fixed by someone who has only read about the control plane. Each region runs at least 4 edge nodes behind a network load balancer. Scaling is manual: there is no autoscaler on the edge tier, on purpose, because a scale event during an incident has bitten us twice.

[8] [id=slack-infra-030 | slack message in #infra | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-03-20]
The runbook floor is 4 edge nodes for a customer facing region and we hold to it, exceptions in writing only.

[9] [id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
Certificates are distributed by the platform team and are the same across all edge nodes in a region. A certificate problem is never a single-node problem: if one node is serving a bad certificate, all of them are, and the fix is a redistribution rather than a restart. The log retention on an edge node is 7 days locally, and everything is shipped to the central store where the retention is the customer's own retention window.

[10] [id=slack-infra-019 | slack message in #infra | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-03-20]
The runbook floor is 4 edge nodes for a customer facing region and we hold to it. Below that a single node failure is customer visible.

[11] [id=slack-eng-core-010 | slack message in #eng-core | by Tomas Ruiz | on 2027-01-07]
The edge nodes are owned by the platform team, and so is edge certificate distribution: everything that pushes a file onto an edge node is ours.

[7] [id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
The Palisade gateway runs on edge nodes in three regions. This runbook covers the edge nodes only: the control plane has its own runbook and the two are deliberately kept apart so an edge problem cannot be fixed by someone who has only read about the control plane. Each region runs at least 4 edge nodes behind a network load balancer. Scaling is manual: there is no autoscaler on the edge tier, on purpose, because a scale event during an incident has bitten us twice.

[8] [id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
To add a node, run the provisioning job with the region flag and wait for the health check to pass twice in a row. Draining a node takes the node out of the load balancer, waits for in-flight requests and then stops the process. The drain timeout is 120 seconds. A node that has not drained by then is killed, and the requests it was serving are lost, so drain during a quiet window if you can choose.

[2] [id=doc-040 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Postmortem policy]
A written postmortem is required for any incident with more than 30 minutes of customer-visible downtime. It is due within 5 working days of the incident closing. An incident with no customer-visible symptom needs a line in the weekly digest and nothing else.

The escalation ladder for an incident that is not moving is: incident commander, then the engineering manager on the affected team, then the VP of engineering. Do not skip a rung, and do not escalate by direct message.

[5] [id=doc-041 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Postmortem policy, threshold]

The Palisade gateway runs on edge nodes in three regions. This runbook covers the edge nodes only: the control plane has its own runbook and the two are deliberately kept apart so an edge problem cannot be fixed by someone who has only read about the control plane. Each region runs at least 4 edge nodes behind a network load balancer. Scaling is manual: there is no autoscaler on the edge tier, on purpose, because a scale event during an incident has bitten us twice.

Draining a node takes the node out of the load balancer, waits for in-flight requests and then stops the process. The drain timeout is 120 seconds. A node that has not drained by then is killed, and the requests it was serving are lost, so drain during a quiet window if you can choose.

These notes are the shape of the pipeline as it is built today, written after the Relay Bridge rename so the names are current. Where an older document says Relay Connect it means the same product. The pipeline has four stages: fetch, normalise, validate and load. Fetch talks to the customer system and is the only stage allowed to make outbound network calls.
